fact_text: A third-country national coming to work in the Netherlands as a highly skilled migrant (kennismigrant) needs an IND residence permit; the permit is applied for by the employer, not the employee.
evidence_quote: To work in the Netherlands as a highly skilled migrant, you need a residence permit.

fact_text: The highly skilled migrant permit requires a minimum gross monthly salary (the salary criterion) set by the IND; the required amount depends on the category (e.g. under 30, 30 or older, reduced criterion) and the migrant must meet the amount that applies on the date of the application.
evidence_quote: The required amounts change every year on January 1. The highly skilled migrant must meet the required amount that applies on the date of the application.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed there is one fixed salary number. Actually the required gross monthly amount differs by category (e.g. under 30 vs 30+ vs reduced criterion) and changes every 1 January; the migrant must meet the amount in force on the application date. Action required: check the current IND required amount for the correct category before signing the contract.

fact_text: A highly skilled migrant permit can only be applied for by an employer that the IND has recognised as a sponsor; recognised sponsors are listed in the IND public register.
evidence_quote: A recognised sponsor is a company, school, or organisation that has been recognised by the IND. A recognised sponsor can apply for a residence permit for, for example, employees, au pairs or students.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed any employer can hire a highly skilled migrant. Actually only an employer the IND has recognised as a sponsor can file the application, and you can verify this in the IND public register of recognised sponsors. Action required: confirm the employer is a recognised sponsor before relying on the HSM route.

fact_text: For paid employment that does not fall under a special scheme, a third-country national needs a single permit (GVVA) that combines the residence permit and the work permit in one document.
evidence_quote: If you want to work in paid employment in the Netherlands, you need a single permit (in Dutch: gecombineerde vergunning verblijf en arbeid or GVVA). The single permit combines the residence permit and the work permit.

fact_text: Applicants for a regular Dutch residence permit generally have to undergo a tuberculosis (TB) test after arriving in the Netherlands; nationals of listed exempt countries, long-term EU residents and recent test-takers do not.
evidence_quote: After you arrive in the Netherlands, you have to be tested for tuberculosis (TB).

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed no medical steps remain once the permit is approved. Actually many regular-permit holders must undergo a post-arrival TB test (nationals of listed countries, long-term EU residents and people tested in NL within 6 months are exempt). Action required: check the IND exemption list; if not exempt, book the test at the municipal health service (GGD).

fact_text: Many third-country nationals also need an MVV (machtiging tot voorlopig verblijf), a Type-D entry visa for stays over 90 days, which is applied for together with the residence permit (usually by the sponsor) and collected before travelling to the Netherlands. Whether an MVV is needed depends on nationality.
evidence_quote: The MVV is an entry visa. This visa is intended for persons who want to stay in the Netherlands for more than 90 days.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed you just get a residence permit and fly over. Actually most nationalities first need an MVV (Type-D entry visa), applied for together with the residence permit and usually submitted by the sponsor, then collected at a Dutch embassy before travel; EU/EEA/Swiss and a short list of countries (e.g. US, UK, Japan, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, South Korea) are exempt. Action required: confirm whether your nationality is MVV-required before booking travel.

fact_text: An EU/EEA or Swiss national does not need a residence permit to live in the Netherlands; the valid EU/EEA passport or ID card is proof of lawful residence and there is no need to register with the IND.
evidence_quote: You do not need a residence permit to live in the Netherlands. Your valid travel document (passport or ID card) issued by an EU/EEA country or Switzerland serves as proof of lawful residence in the Netherlands. You do not need to register with the IND.

fact_text: An EU/EEA or Swiss national is free to work in the Netherlands and the employer does not need a work permit (tewerkstellingsvergunning, TWV).
evidence_quote: You are free to work in the Netherlands. Your employer does not need a work permit (in Dutch: tewerkstellingsvergunning or TWV).

fact_text: An EU/EEA national who will live in the Netherlands longer than 4 months must register in person at their municipality (in the Personal Records Database, BRP); registration is what issues the citizen service number (BSN), and you must register within 5 days of arriving.
evidence_quote: You will be given a citizen service number (BSN) when you register.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed EU citizens have nothing to arrange. Actually you must still register in person at your municipality (BRP) within 5 days of arriving if you stay longer than 4 months; this registration is what issues your BSN. Action required: book a gemeente appointment on arrival — the BSN gates salary payment, banking, tax and healthcare.

fact_text: A third-country national who will live in the Netherlands longer than 4 months must register in person at their municipality (in the Personal Records Database, BRP) to receive the citizen service number (BSN); registration requires being legally resident, so the residence permit may be needed first.
evidence_quote: You will be given a citizen service number (BSN) when you register.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed the residence permit is all you need. Actually you must also register at your municipality (BRP) to get a BSN, and you can only register once you are legally resident — you may need the residence permit first. Action required: register within 5 days of arrival; without a BSN you cannot be paid, bank or take out insurance.

fact_text: To arrange Dutch government, tax, healthcare and pension matters online, an EU/EEA resident needs a DigiD, the national digital identity login; a DigiD can only be obtained after you have a BSN.
evidence_quote: Your DigiD allows you to identify yourself when making arrangements on the internet, such as with the government, educational institutes, healthcare institutions or your pension fund.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed you can handle Dutch admin online straight away. Actually almost every government, tax, healthcare and pension service requires a DigiD login, and you can only apply for a DigiD after you have a BSN; the activation code is sent by post and takes several days. Action required: apply for DigiD right after municipal registration.

fact_text: To arrange Dutch government, tax, healthcare and pension matters online, a third-country resident needs a DigiD, the national digital identity login; a DigiD can only be obtained after you have a BSN.
evidence_quote: Your DigiD allows you to identify yourself when making arrangements on the internet, such as with the government, educational institutes, healthcare institutions or your pension fund.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed you can handle Dutch admin online straight away. Actually almost every government, tax, healthcare and pension service requires a DigiD login, and you can only apply for a DigiD after you have a BSN; the activation code is sent by post and takes several days. Action required: apply for DigiD right after municipal registration.

fact_text: An EU/EEA national who comes to live or work in the Netherlands must take out Dutch health insurance and must do so no later than 4 months after arriving; cover applies from the arrival date.
evidence_quote: If you come to live or work in the Netherlands you need to take out Dutch health insurance as quickly as possible. And no later than 4 months after arriving.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed existing EU/foreign cover is enough or that there is plenty of time. Actually you must take out Dutch insurance with cover backdated to your arrival date; you have 4 months to arrange it but cover is NOT retroactive if you are late, and the CAK can fine you. Action required: buy a Dutch basisverzekering as soon as you have a BSN.

fact_text: A third-country national who comes to live or work in the Netherlands must take out Dutch health insurance and must do so no later than 4 months after arriving; cover applies from the arrival date.
evidence_quote: If you come to live or work in the Netherlands you need to take out Dutch health insurance as quickly as possible. And no later than 4 months after arriving.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed existing foreign cover is enough or that there is plenty of time. Actually you must take out Dutch insurance with cover backdated to your arrival date; you have 4 months to arrange it but cover is NOT retroactive if you are late, and the CAK can fine you. Action required: buy a Dutch basisverzekering as soon as you have a BSN.

fact_text: An EU/EEA employee recruited from outside the Netherlands may be able to use the Expat Scheme (30% facility), a payroll-tax facility, if all the Tax Administration's conditions are met (including specific expertise, recruitment from abroad and a valid decision); it is applied for together with the employer.
evidence_quote: You can apply for the Expat Scheme if you meet all the conditions.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed the tax break is automatic. Actually the Expat Scheme (30% facility) must be applied for jointly by employer and employee and is granted only on a valid decision, for staff recruited from abroad with specific expertise. Action required: request the application early — it is time-limited and the rules have changed in recent years; confirm current terms with a tax adviser.

fact_text: A third-country employee recruited from outside the Netherlands may be able to use the Expat Scheme (30% facility), a payroll-tax facility, if all the Tax Administration's conditions are met (including specific expertise, recruitment from abroad and a valid decision); it is applied for together with the employer.
evidence_quote: You can apply for the Expat Scheme if you meet all the conditions.

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed the tax break is automatic. fact_text: Once an EU/EEA national becomes a Dutch tax resident, they must declare their worldwide income in their Dutch income-tax return; double taxation is then relieved under the applicable tax treaty.
evidence_quote: You have to state your worldwide income

applies_to.non_obvious_note: Commonly believed you are taxed only on Dutch earnings. Actually once you are a Dutch tax resident you must declare your worldwide income in the Dutch return; double taxation is relieved under the applicable tax treaty rather than by excluding foreign income. Action required: get advice on your residency start date and treaty position.
